questions.q: Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction between dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium carbonate. Name all three products formed.
questions.a: Na₂CO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). Products: sodium chloride (salt), water, carbon dioxide. A wrong answer where the student writes only NaCl + CO₂ (missing H₂O) reveals they do not understand that the carbonate ion (CO₃²⁻) combines with 2H⁺ to form H₂CO₃ which decomposes to H₂O + CO₂. Missing water violates mass conservation and is a common 1-mark deduction in board exams.

questions.q: Explain why the reaction of sulfuric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate requires only half the moles of acid compared to sodium carbonate for the same amount of CO₂ production.
questions.a: NaHCO₃ contains one replaceable H⁺ equivalent (HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂CO₃ → H₂O + CO₂) while CO₃²⁻ requires two H⁺ (CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂CO₃ → H₂O + CO₂). Thus 1 mol H₂SO₄ (2H⁺) reacts with 2 mol NaHCO₃ but only 1 mol Na₂CO₃. A wrong answer stating "both need 2H⁺" reveals confusion between the anion charges and failure to apply valency cross-method from Class 9 (c9_chem_ch3_6) to acid-base stoichiometry.

questions.q: A student adds dilute HCl to a white solid X. A colourless gas Y evolves which turns lime water milky. The residue after reaction dissolves completely in water giving a neutral solution. Identify X and Y, and write the balanced equation.
questions.a: X = CaCO₃ (calcium carbonate), Y = CO₂. Equation: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). Steps: (1) Gas turns lime water milky → CO₂. (2) Residue dissolves giving neutral solution → CaCl₂ (salt of strong acid + strong base). (3) Balance: Ca and Cl balanced with 2HCl, H and O balanced with H₂O. A wrong answer identifying X as Na₂CO₃ reveals inability to use solubility/residue clues — Na₂CO₃ would also dissolve but the "white solid" description fits both; however, CaCO₃ is the classic "limestone" example in NCERT. Missing (s) and (aq) state symbols loses ½ mark in board exams.

questions.q: Compare the volume of CO₂ gas produced at STP when 10 g of Na₂CO₃ and 10 g of NaHCO₃ are reacted separately with excess dilute HCl. Which gives more CO₂ and by what factor? (Molar masses: Na₂CO₃ = 106 g/mol, NaHCO₃ = 84 g/mol)
questions.a: Na₂CO₃: 10 g = 0.0943 mol → produces 0.0943 mol CO₂ (1:1). NaHCO₃: 10 g = 0.119 mol → produces 0.119 mol CO₂ (1:1). NaHCO₃ gives more CO₂ by factor 0.119/0.0943 ≈ 1.26. A wrong answer claiming Na₂CO₃ gives more because "it has 2 Na" reveals confusion between formula units and mole concept (c9_chem_ch3_9). Students must calculate moles first, then use stoichiometry — mass alone is misleading due to different molar masses.

questions.q: A student writes the reaction: 2NaHCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2CO₂ + 2H₂O. Evaluate if this equation is correctly balanced and chemically accurate. If not, correct it.
questions.a: The equation is correctly balanced: Na (2), H (2+2=4 on left, 4 on right), C (2), O (6+4=10 left, 4+4+2=10 right), S (1). Chemically accurate: H₂SO₄ provides 2H⁺, each NaHCO₃ needs 1H⁺ → 2:1 ratio correct. A wrong answer saying "should be NaHCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + CO₂ + H₂O" reveals misunderstanding that with excess acid, complete neutralisation to normal salt (Na₂SO₄) occurs. Board exams expect complete reaction unless "limited acid" is specified.

questions.q: Design a simple laboratory experiment to distinguish between solid samples of sodium carbonate and sodium hydrogencarbonate using only dilute HCl and lime water. Write the procedure, expected observations, and the chemical reasoning.
questions.a: Procedure: (1) Take two test tubes, add 1 g each solid. (2) Add 5 mL dilute HCl to both. (3) Pass gas from each through separate lime water tubes. Observations: Both produce CO₂ (lime water turns milky). Na₂CO₃ reacts vigorously with 2HCl; NaHCO₃ reacts moderately with 1HCl per mole. To distinguish: measure gas volume — same mass of NaHCO₃ gives ~1.26× more CO₂ (see Q4). Or add acid dropwise: Na₂CO₃ needs 2× more drops for complete reaction. Reasoning: Different H⁺ stoichiometry (CO₃²⁻ vs HCO₃⁻). A poor answer that only says "both fizz" without quantitative distinction reveals inability to apply mole concept for identification — a common board practical question.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: When an acid reacts with a metal carbonate (CO₃²⁻) or metal ______ (HCO₃⁻), it produces a salt, water, and carbon dioxide gas.
Fill in the blank: Observe what happens when you drop a few drops of vinegar (acetic acid) on baking soda (sodium ______) in your kitchen — vigorous fizzing occurs due to CO₂ gas.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can write balanced chemical equations for any acid-carbonate/hydrogencarbonate reaction, identify all three products correctly, and describe the lime water test for CO₂ with the correct observation and equation.
